title: Authentication and Connecting to APIs Securely
summary: Almost every real API requires you to prove who you are before it will give or accept data, so authentication is a daily part of automation work. The simplest method is an API key - a long secret string you include in your request (often in a header
content:
# Authentication and Connecting to APIs Securely ##### The API key in the screenshot In 2023 a developer posted a tutorial screenshot showing their working API integration. Beautiful workflow, clean data, one small problem: the request URL in the corner of the image read `?api_key=sk_live_4f8a...`. Within a day, automated scrapers that watch public repositories and image posts had found it and started using it. The bill arrived at the end of the month. This happens constantly. GitHub's own secret-scanning service detects and revokes millions of leaked credentials a year — which tells you both how common the mistake is and how aggressively bots hunt for it. **Authentication** is how an API knows who you are; **authorization** is what you are allowed to do once it knows. Every real integration you build depends on both, and handling credentials carelessly is the fastest way to turn a helpful automation into a security incident. Today you learn the four methods you will meet, how automation tools store secrets, and the rules that keep you out of that story. ##### API keys: the simplest method An **API key** is a long random string the service gives you: `sk_live_9f2b7c41a83e...`. You include it with every request, and the service looks it up to identify your account. It usually travels in a header: ```bash # Header — the correct, standard placement curl "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?q=Pune" \ -H "X-API-Key: YOUR_API_KEY_HERE_xxxxxxxxxxxx" ``` Some older services accept it as a query parameter instead: ```bash # Query parameter — works, but avoid when you have the choice curl "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?q=Pune&appid=YOUR_API_KEY_HERE" ``` Why prefer the header? Query strings are logged. They appear in web server access logs, proxy logs, browser history, `Referer` headers, and analytics. A key in a header stays out of most of those. If the API only supports a query parameter (OpenWeather does), that is fine — just be extra careful about screenshots and shared logs. API keys are simple, which is their strength and their weakness. **Anyone holding the key has your access**, there is usually no user-level granularity, and rotating a key means updating every place it is used. Good services let you create multiple keys with descriptive names and separate scopes so you can revoke one without breaking everything. ##### Bearer tokens and Basic auth **Bearer tokens** are the most common pattern in modern APIs. The name means exactly what it says: whoever bears this token gets the access. ```http Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9... ``` The token might be a simple opaque string or a **JWT** (JSON Web Token) — a signed, base64-encoded object containing claims like user ID, scopes and an expiry timestamp. The important practical difference from an API key is that bearer tokens are usually **short-lived**: they expire in an hour or a day, and you refresh them. That limits the damage window if one leaks. **Basic auth** is the oldest scheme. You send a username and password, joined by a colon and base64-encoded: ```bash # These two are equivalent curl -u "myuser:mypassword" https://api.example.com/v1/data curl https://api.example.com/v1/data \ -H "Authorization: Basic bXl1c2VyOm15cGFzc3dvcmQ=" ``` Understand this clearly: **base64 is encoding, not encryption.** Anyone who intercepts that header can decode it back to your password in one step. Basic auth is only acceptable over HTTPS, and even then it is a legacy pattern. Many APIs that nominally use Basic auth actually expect an API key as the username and a blank password — Stripe works this way. ##### OAuth 2.0: the "Login with..." model When you clicked "Sign in with Google" inside Zapier or n8n, you used **OAuth 2.0** (specified in RFC 6749). It solves a problem the previous methods cannot. The problem: you want Zapier to read your Google Sheets. With an API key model, you would have to hand Zapier your Google password — giving it access to your Gmail, Drive, Photos, everything, forever, with no way to revoke it short of changing your password. OAuth's insight is to introduce a **delegated, scoped, revocable** grant. Instead of sharing your password, you authorize a limited token. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant U as You participant Z as Zapier participant G as Google (auth server) participant A as Google Sheets API U->>Z: "Connect Google Sheets" Z->>U: redirect to Google's consent page U->>G: log in ON GOOGLE'S SITE, approve scopes G->>Z: redirect back with a short-lived auth code Z->>G: exchange code + client secret for tokens G-->>Z: access token (1 hr) + refresh token Z->>A: API call with Bearer access token A-->>Z: spreadsheet data Note over Z,G: when the access token expires,
Zapier silently uses the refresh token ``` Four properties make this materially more secure than sharing a key: 1. **Your password never reaches the third party.** You type it only on Google's own domain. 2. **Scopes limit access.** The consent screen listing "See, edit, create and delete your spreadsheets" is the scope set. Sheets access does not imply Gmail access. 3. **Access tokens are short-lived** — typically one hour — so a leaked token expires quickly. The longer-lived refresh token is used only to get new access tokens. 4. **You can revoke it independently.** Google's account settings let you disconnect Zapier without touching your password or any other app. The cost is complexity: OAuth requires a registered application, a client ID and secret, redirect URLs, and token refresh logic. That is precisely why automation platforms are valuable — Zapier, Make and n8n implement all of it, and you experience it as one button. The one case where you do the work yourself is connecting an API n8n does not know natively. Then you register an app in the provider's developer console, set the redirect URI n8n gives you, and paste the client ID and secret into an OAuth2 credential. ##### Storing credentials in automation tools Every platform you have learned has a dedicated, encrypted **credential store**, deliberately separated from workflow definitions. - **Zapier** — *App Connections*. Reusable across Zaps, named, revocable individually. - **Make.com** — *Connections*, managed per app, shareable within a team. - **n8n** — *Credentials*, encrypted at rest with a key from the `N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY` environment variable. Self-hosted users can also inject secrets via environment variables and reference them as `{{$env.MY_API_KEY}}`. The architectural point that matters: **credentials are stored separately from workflows**. When you export an n8n workflow as JSON to share it, credentials are referenced by name, not embedded. That separation only protects you if you use the store — typing a key directly into an HTTP node's header field defeats it entirely, and that key *will* end up in your export. Three rules follow directly: **Never hard-code.** Not in a URL, not in a header value, not in a Code node, not in a comment. **Never commit or share.** No screenshots, no Slack pastes, no repositories. Add `.env` to `.gitignore` before you write a single secret into it. **Rotate and scope.** Use separate credentials per environment (dev/prod) and per client, with the minimum scopes needed. When someone leaves the team or a key is exposed, revoke rather than hope. Add a fourth for the real world: **use test/sandbox keys while building.** Stripe, Razorpay and most serious APIs provide them. Building against live payment credentials is how people accidentally charge real cards during a test. ##### Rate limits and API best practices Authentication gets you in; **rate limits** govern how often you may knock. A service might allow 60 requests per minute, 1,000 per hour, or 10,000 per day, usually tied to your key. You discover your standing from response headers: ```http HTTP/1.1 200 OK X-RateLimit-Limit: 5000 X-RateLimit-Remaining: 4998 X-RateLimit-Reset: 1773481200 ``` Exceed the limit and you get **`429 Too Many Requests`**, often with a `Retry-After` header telling you exactly how many seconds to wait. Respect it — hammering a rate-limited endpoint can get your key suspended entirely. Practices that keep you in good standing: - **Read the docs' rate-limit section before building**, not after your first 429. - **Batch where the API allows it** — one request creating 100 records beats 100 requests. - **Use webhooks instead of polling** when available; it eliminates the wasteful calls entirely. - **Add delays in loops.** Make's Sleep module, n8n's Wait node and Zapier's Delay exist for this. - **Implement exponential backoff** on 429 and 5xx: wait 1s, then 2s, 4s, 8s. n8n's *Retry On Fail* and Make's error-handler directives do this for you. - **Cache responses that rarely change.** Fetching a country list on every run is wasted quota. ##### Common pitfalls - **`401` vs `403` confusion.** 401 means your credential is missing, malformed or expired. 403 means it is valid but lacks permission — usually a missing scope, so re-authorize with the right one. - **Expired OAuth connections.** Password changes and revoked grants break every workflow using them. Watch the platform's error emails. - **Wrong header name.** `X-API-Key` vs `Authorization` vs `apikey` — copy exactly from the docs, they are case-insensitive but not interchangeable. - **Missing `Bearer ` prefix.** `Authorization: eyJhbGc...` fails; `Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGc...` works. - **Keys in URLs that end up in logs and screenshots.** - **Using one key everywhere.** Rotating it then breaks fourteen workflows simultaneously. - **Ignoring 429s.** Retrying immediately makes the problem worse. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task has two halves and both matter. First, get a free API key from a service such as **OpenWeather**, and make an authenticated request with the key in the correct place — confirm you get real data back, then deliberately break the key and observe the `401`. Seeing both outcomes teaches more than seeing one. Second, connect an **OAuth app** (Google is easiest) inside n8n or Make, and read the consent screen carefully before approving. Then go to your Google account's "Third-party apps with account access" page and see your own grant listed there. The mini project combines both methods in one automation: authenticate to two APIs — one with a key/token, one with OAuth — fetch from each, and combine the results, with **every credential stored in the tool's credential manager**. Zero secrets typed into node parameters. For the assignment, explain **API key vs OAuth**, why OAuth is safer for third-party connections (delegation, scopes, expiry, independent revocation), and list three credential-handling rules. Write it as advice you would give a teammate; it doubles as a portfolio piece showing you take security seriously. ##### Key takeaways - API keys are simple shared secrets — prefer headers over query parameters, and treat them exactly like passwords. - Bearer tokens are the modern default and usually expire; Basic auth is base64-encoded, not encrypted, and is legacy. - OAuth 2.0 delegates scoped, expiring, independently revocable access without sharing your password — which is why every serious platform uses it. - Always store secrets in the platform's credential manager, never in node parameters, URLs, screenshots or repositories. - Respect rate limits: read the headers, batch, cache, prefer webhooks, and back off exponentially on 429 and 5xx.
